###### Abstract

Long chain-of-thought (Long-CoT) reasoning improves accuracy in LLMs,
yet its verbose, self-reflective style often hinders effective
distillation into small language models (SLMs). We revisit Long-CoT
compression through the lens of capability alignment and ask: Can
pruning improve reasoning? We propose Prune-on-Logic, a structure-aware
framework that transforms Long-CoT into logic graphs and selectively
prunes low-utility reasoning steps under self-verification constraints.
Through systematic analysis across three pruning strategies—targeting
entire chains, core reasoning, and verification, we find that
verification pruning consistently improves accuracy while reducing token
usage, whereas pruning reasoning steps or indiscriminate pruning
degrades performance. Our study reveals that effective pruning aligns
supervision with model capacity rather than merely shortening inputs.
Gains hold across tasks, model scales, and CoT capability, with larger
models benefiting more from pruning due to richer but more redundant
reasoning. Our empirical findings highlight pruning as a structural
optimization strategy for aligning CoT reasoning with SLM capacity.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs), including OpenAI-O1 [Jaech et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib10) and Deepseek-R1 [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6), have
demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning across
mathematical problem-solving [Zhang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib38) and
logical reasoning [Wan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib26). These models have
evolved from Short Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning with concise,
stepwise logic [Wei et al. (2022)](#bib.bib28); [Yang et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib31); [Wu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29) to Long-CoT
reasoning with deeper chains [Jin et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12); [Jiang
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib11) via iterative exploration [Bi et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib2); [Yang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib32) and reflection
[Zhang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib38). While Long-CoT reasoning
significantly boosts reasoning capacity, it also introduces considerable
computational overhead, with extended reasoning chains amplifying
inference latency, memory demands driven by key-value caching, and the
quadratic computational cost of attention [Zhang et al.
(2025c)](#bib.bib37)—effects that are magnified by both model scaling
[Zhang et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib34); [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6) and
test-time thinking scaling [Yang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib32), severely
limiting LLMs’ effectiveness in real-world complex reasoning tasks under
long-thought reasoning pattern.

To address these resource constraints, recent research has increasingly
focused on transferring the Long-CoT reasoning abilities of large-scale
language models into Smaller Language Models (SLMs) via CoT distillation
[Ranaldi and Freitas (2024)](#bib.bib22); [Bi et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib1)
to perform complex long-context reasoning with greater efficiency
[Shridhar et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23); [Ranaldi and Freitas
(2024)](#bib.bib22); [Li et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib15). However, a key
challenge remains: SLMs face inherent limitations in acquiring
long-context reasoning due to their smaller capacities. Unlike
traditional distillation approaches, which primarily focus on
performance, recent work emphasizes how SLMs can learn to perform
complex long-context reasoning despite their capacity constraints [Li
et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib16). Token-level compression via prompting [Xia
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib30) or LLMLingua [Pan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib20)
has been shown to be lossy for finetuning [Han et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7)
or RLHF [Hou et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8), frequently discarding critical
information necessary for accurate long-context reasoning [Zhang et al.
(2025c)](#bib.bib37). While existing approaches such as
length-harmonizing decoding [Luo et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib18) and hybrid
training on mixed-length data [Li et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib16) improve
the likelihood of generating long or short CoT outputs, they largely
focus on output preferences rather than fundamentally enhancing SLMs’
ability to learn from long-CoT reasoning.

In this work, we revisit long-CoT compression from a capability-centric
perspective and ask: Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Instead of
compressing at the token level, we investigate whether pruning logically
redundant or minimally impactful reasoning steps can enhance SLMs’
ability to perform long-context reasoning more effectively. Our goal is
to distill not just shorter outputs, but more efficient and cognitively
meaningful reasoning paths that align better with SLM’s limited
capacity. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose Prune-on-Logic, a structure-aware compression framework
  that transforms Long-CoT into logic graphs and enables selective
  pruning of low-utility reasoning steps, guided by loss-based
  importance scoring.
- •
  We conduct a systematic comparison of three pruning
  strategies—All-chain, Reasoning-only, and Verification-only—and reveal
  that pruning all verification steps consistently improves accuracy and
  reduces inference cost, while other strategies degrade performance.
- •
  We reveal that pruning logic-bearing nodes, particularly within the
  verification phase, enhances reasoning effectiveness in SLMs. This
  aligns the reasoning process with model capacity and capability,
  offering a robust mechanism for scalable Long-CoT distillation.

## 2 Related Work

#### LLM as a Graph Parser.

To better manage long CoT reasoning, we decompose the original long CoT
into a step-level logic graph for structured reasoning, following
[Pandey et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21). Recent advances in structured
reasoning via CoT [Zhang et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib36); [Zhang et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib35) and self-correction [Zhang et al.
(2025d)](#bib.bib39) have improved LLM-based parsers and revealed their
ability to represent logical structures as graph-based reasoning
processes [Luo et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19). Unlike prior methods that
extract isolated sub-information, we preserve the original sentence’s
logical flow by decomposing it into ordered reasoning steps. Each step
undergoes a verification phase to maintain fidelity to the original
content. This design yields a semantically equivalent and structurally
organized representation.

![Refer to caption](2505.14582v3/Prune-on-Logic2.png)

Figure 2: Overview of the Prune-on-Logic framework. Given a Long-CoT
sequence, we build a logic graph that captures deductive dependencies
and, through self-pruning under logical equivalence constraints, scores
and eliminates low-impact reasoning steps. We explore three pruning
strategies—All-chain, Reasoning-only, and Verification-only—and
fine-tune SLMs on the compressed CoTs to enhance both efficiency and
reasoning robustness.

#### Long2short CoT Compression for SLMs.

Existing compression methods for SLMs are inherently lossy. Fine-tuning
token-level compression via perplexity [Han et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7),
prompting strategies [Hou et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8), step-level
compression [Zhang et al. (2025c)](#bib.bib37), or RLHF on
length-harmonizing datasets [Luo et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib18) often
degrade reasoning capabilities. As shown in
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"),
existing methods, while improving efficiency, risk discarding critical
reasoning information [Hou et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8) necessary for
complex tasks. Our work primarily revisits how step-level compression
can enhance SLMs. As such, we do not consider comparisons with
alternative approaches such as data mixing tricky strategies [Li et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib16) or budget prompting strategies [Han et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib7). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work
to systematically explore perplexity-aware step-level pruning, offering
new insights into how lossy pruning affects different CoT stages (e.g.,
reasoning, verification).

## 3 Prune-on-Logic

Inspired by the complex graph-like connectivity in biological brains
[Friston (2008)](#bib.bib4), we adopt a structure-aware view of
reasoning data following the advice of [Zhang et al.
(2025c)](#bib.bib37); [Luo et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19). We propose
Prune-on-Logic involving: (1) logic graph construction
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Equivalent Logic Graph Reconstruction ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")),
(2) step-level importance scoring via predictive loss and ranking-based
pruning of low-impact steps
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).
We systematically explore three pruning strategies over different
reasoning phases, aiming to compress Long-CoT without degrading
inference quality, and revisit the question: Can pruning improve
reasoning, when compression is guided not by length but by capability
alignment? These strategies target different phases of the reasoning
process: full sequences, core derivations, and verification tails. This
allows us to probe not only where pruning is most effective, but also
what should be pruned.

Specifically, we explore two granularities of pruning: (1) removing
individual logic nodes, which represent discrete reasoning steps, and
(2) removing edges, i.e., weakening or severing weakly informative
logical connections between steps. This distinction is important:
pruning a node removes its content entirely, while pruning an edge
changes the dependency structure and may isolate redundant subchains. By
analyzing both forms of pruning across different reasoning roles, we
revisit a fundamental question: Can logic-aware pruning compress CoT
traces not by truncation, but by selectively removing parts that least
support inference—across steps, stages, and rhetorical roles?

### 3.1 Equivalent Logic Graph Reconstruction

Long chain-of-thought (Long-CoT) sequences often contain rich,
multi-step reasoning interleaved with rhetorical scaffolding [Friston
(2008)](#bib.bib4). While their original form is linear, the underlying
logic is inherently graph-structured [Luo et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19).
To make such structure explicit without altering the content, following
[Luo et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19), we map each CoT sequence as a
semantically equivalent logic graph that preserves all deductive steps
but encodes them as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). This transformation
does not alter the meaning of the reasoning; rather, it restructures the
sentence-level logic into a graph topology that reflects the actual flow
of inference.

### 3.2 Equivalent Logic Graph Reconstruction

Long chain-of-thought (Long-CoT) sequences encode rich, multi-step
reasoning in a linear textual form. However, their underlying semantic
structure is inherently graph-based [Luo et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19). To
reveal this structure without altering the original content, we
transform each CoT into a semantically equivalent directed acyclic graph
(DAG), denoted as $`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{E})`$, where nodes
represent deductive steps and edges denote logical dependencies.

#### Logic Unit Segmentation.

Given a CoT sequence $`\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{n}\}`$, we
prompt a large language model (LLM) to segment it into two disjoint
subsets using a classification prompt $`P_{\text{logic}}`$ (see
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Logic Unit Segmentation Prompt (𝑃_{𝑙⁢𝑜⁢𝑔⁢𝑖⁢𝑐}) ‣ Appendix A Prompt Details for Equivalent Logic Graph ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")):

- •
  $`\mathcal{N}`$: original sentences that express reasoning or
  verification steps, such as symbolic operations, numerical
  derivations, or inference-bearing conclusions;
- •
  $`\mathcal{C}`$: original sentences that function as rhetorical
  connectors, including fillers, transitions, or metacognitive phrases.

This yields a structured annotation of the original sequence:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{LLM}(\mathcal{S};P_{\text{logic}})
``` |  | (1) |

Each sentence is assigned a role label, and its original position is
preserved for downstream reference.

0:  CoT sequence $`\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{n}\}`$, pruning
ratio $`\gamma\in(0,1)`$, pre-Sft LLM $`\mathcal{SLM}`$

0:  Pruned sequence $`\mathcal{S}_{{pruned}}`$

1:  Node Segmentation: Partition $`\mathcal{S}`$ into logic steps
$`\mathcal{N}`$ and rhetorical links $`\mathcal{C}`$

2:  Graph Extraction: Construct latent DAG
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})`$ by selecting minimal support
sets $`F_{i}`$ for each $`n_{i}\in\mathcal{N}`$
(Eq. [3](#S3.E3 "In Node Connection Assignment. ‣ 3.2 Equivalent Logic Graph Reconstruction ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"))
and assigning edge for each connection $`c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}`$

3:  Pruning Candidate Identification: Extract linear candidates
$`\mathcal{N}_{{prune}}\subseteq\mathcal{N}`$ such that
$`|F_{n_{i}}|=1`$ and $`|T_{n_{i}}|=1`$

4:  for all $`n_{i}\in\mathcal{N}_{{prune}}`$ do

5:   Let $`to_{i}`$ be the successor of $`n_{i}`$

6:   Define step span $`[p_{\text{st}},p_{\text{ed}}]`$ from $`n_{i}`$
to $`to_{i}`$

7:   Compute semantic utility $`\text{Score}_{i}`$ using
$`\mathcal{SLM}`$
(Eq. [4](#S3.Ex1 "In 3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")–[5](#S3.Ex2 "In 3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"))

8:  end for

9:  Score Ranking: Sort $`\mathcal{N}_{prune}`$ by $`\text{Score}_{i}`$
in ascending order.

10:  Step Selection: Prune
top-$`k=\lfloor\gamma\cdot|\mathcal{N}|\rfloor`$ low-impact nodes from
$`\mathcal{N}_{{prune}}`$

11:  Sequence Reconstruction: Form $`\mathcal{S}_{{pruned}}`$ by
removing pruned steps from $`\mathcal{S}`$ while preserving original
step order

12:  return $`\mathcal{S}_{{pruned}}`$

Algorithm 1 Logic-Aware Self-Pruning

#### Node Connection Assignment.

Based on the segmented units, we construct a logic graph
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})`$, where
$`\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{N}`$ and $`\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{E}`$. For
each reasoning node $`n_{i}\in\mathcal{N}`$, we prompt the LLM (via
$`P_{{conn}}`$ detailed in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Node Connection Assignment Prompt (𝑃_{𝑐⁢𝑜⁢𝑛⁢𝑛}) ‣ Appendix A Prompt Details for Equivalent Logic Graph ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"))
to select a minimal set of prior nodes
$`F_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{<i}`$ that justify its derivation. This
induces a directed edge set:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{E}=\bigcup_{n_{i}\in\mathcal{N}}\{(f,n_{i})\mid f\in F_{i}\}
``` |  | (2) |

where support sets are predicted via:

|     |                                                        |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       F_{i}=\mathcal{LLM}(n_{i};\mathcal{N}_{<i},P_{{conn}})
       ```                                                     |     | (3) |

Subsequently, we map each connection to a graph edge, assuming its
target node is the immediate successor in the text sequence. To improve
connection accuracy, we incorporate a self-verification step in which
the LLM is re-prompted to reassess or validate each predicted $`F_{i}`$.
This iterative check enhances robustness against spurious links and
promotes logical coherence detailed in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Node Connection Assignment Prompt (𝑃_{𝑐⁢𝑜⁢𝑛⁢𝑛}) ‣ Appendix A Prompt Details for Equivalent Logic Graph ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning").
The resulting graph $`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})`$ not only
reconstructs the latent deductive structure of the original CoT sequence
but also records explicit mappings between graph nodes and their
corresponding sentence indices. This enables symbolic reasoning and
text-level alignment to be jointly exploited in downstream tasks. We
adopt the semantic equivalence hypothesis [Luo et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib19)—that $`\mathcal{G}`$ faithfully preserves the full
deductive semantics of $`\mathcal{S}`$—as further detailed in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Semantic Equivalence ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning").

### 3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking

Building on the constructed logic graph
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})`$, we further introduce a
loss-based ranking mechanism [Pan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib20) that
estimates each node’s semantic contribution via token-level perplexity
difference. Importantly, we restrict pruning to nodes that (1) have
exactly one predecessor and successor in $`\mathcal{G}`$; (2) form a
linear inference segment.

Let $`n_{i}`$ be a candidate node and $`to_{i}`$ its immediate successor
in $`\mathcal{G}`$. We define the span $`[p_{\text{st}},p_{\text{ed}}]`$
as the sentence range covering $`n_{i}`$ through $`to_{i}`$. To assess
the semantic contribution of $`n_{i}`$, we compute token-level
perplexity over this span using a frozen pre-SFT small language model
$`\mathcal{SLM}`$:

Perplexity with node retained:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{PPL}_{\textit{retain}}=\exp\Bigg(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\sum_{j=p_{\text{st}}}^{p_{\text{ed}}}\sum_{k=1}^{t_{j}}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad-\log P(tok_{jk}\mid s_{<j},\{tok_{jl}\}_{l<k};\mathcal{SLM})\Bigg)`$ |  | (4) |

Perplexity with node pruned:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{PPL}_{\textit{prune}}=\exp\Bigg(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\sum_{j=p_{\text{st}}}^{p_{\text{ed}}}\sum_{k=1}^{t_{j}}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad-\log P(tok_{jk}\mid s_{<j}\setminus n_{i},\{tok_{jl}\}_{l<k};\mathcal{SLM})\Bigg)`$ |  | (5) |

Then, the self-pruning semantic utility score is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textit{Score}_{i}=\mathcal{PPL}_{{prune}}-\mathcal{PPL}_{{retain}}
``` |  | (6) |

Here, $`\textit{Score}_{i}`$ reflects how much the removal of $`n_{i}`$
degrades the model’s ability to predict downstream tokens. Lower scores
indicate that $`n_{i}`$ contributes little to semantic continuity and
may be safely pruned. We sort all eligible nodes by
$`\textit{Score}_{i}`$ and remove the top-$`k`$ lowest, where
$`k=\lfloor\gamma\cdot|\mathcal{N}|\rfloor`$ and $`\gamma`$ is a pruning
ratio hyperparameter and get the final pruned CoT $`S_{pruned}`$ (See
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 An example of Pruning-on-Logic Data ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
for a Prune-on-Logic data example.)

#### Pruning Strategies.

To explore how pruning affects reasoning, we define three logic-aware
strategies based on functional roles of nodes in the CoT process. The
All-chain strategy removes low-scoring nodes from the entire logic
graph, balancing breadth and depth of reasoning. This acts as a general
compression baseline. The Reasoning-only strategy prunes derivational
steps—such as intermediate calculations—while preserving final
conclusions and verification. This reflects a conservative approach that
favors robustness over maximal compression. Conversely, the
Verification-only strategy targets self-checking or reflective
utterances (e.g., “Let’s verify that”), aiming to reduce rhetorical
redundancy while leaving the computational core intact. Each strategy
produces a pruned sequence $`\mathcal{S}_{{pruned}}`$ by deleting
selected nodes from the original CoT $`\mathcal{S}`$ in order. The
number of deletions is controlled by a pruning ratio $`\gamma\in(0,1)`$,
which determines the top-$`k`$ nodes to remove based on their semantic
utility scores
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).
This explicit control allows us to examine not only *where* pruning is
most effective, but also *how much* pruning can be tolerated before
degrading reasoning quality.

#### Pruning Component.

Beyond determining where to prune within the reasoning process, we also
consider what to prune. Specifically, we explore two levels of
granularity: node-level and connection-level pruning. These correspond
to distinct components of a CoT sequence.

- •
  Node-level pruning removes entire reasoning steps
  $`n_{i}\in\mathcal{N}`$, such as symbolic derivations and their
  corresponding connections.
- •
  Connection-level pruning suppresses rhetorical units
  $`c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}`$, such as discourse fillers and stylistic
  transitions.

Both types are evaluated under the same loss-based scoring mechanism
introduced in
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning").
For each candidate unit, we compute its semantic utility
$`\textit{Score}_{i}`$ using the differential loss with and without the
unit. This unified formulation enables selective removal of both
deductive and rhetorical components. Rhetorical connections are retained
only when their removal would harm the model’s predictive confidence.
Together, the two pruning axes—strategy scope
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"))
and component granularity—form a unified, structure-aware framework.
This design allows us to ask: *What parts of a reasoning chain can be
removed without impairing performance, and how does this vary under
different resource constraints?*

## 4 Experiment

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Models and Datasets.

To investigate whether pruning Long CoT enhances SLM reasoning, we
experiment on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6), comparing
three pruning strategies applied at different reasoning stages
(all-chains, reasoning chains, and verification pruning) under pruning
ratios {0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0}, with the original supervised fine-tuning
(SFT) model as the baseline. Following [Zhang et al.
(2025c)](#bib.bib37), we perform LoRA [Hu et al. (2022)](#bib.bib9) on
Bespoke-Stratos-17k dataset [Labs (2025)](#bib.bib13) for training and
evaluate models on in-domain test sets (AMC 2023 [Li et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib14), AIME [Li et al. (2024)](#bib.bib14),
MATH500 [Lightman et al. (2023)](#bib.bib17)) and out-of-domain test
sets (GSM8K [Cobbe et al. (2021)](#bib.bib3), Big-Bench Hard [Suzgun
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24)). Additionally, we expand verification
pruning to (1) CommonsenseQA [Talmor et al. (2019)](#bib.bib25) for
transfer to non-math reasoning, (2) Llama3.1-8B-Instruct [Grattafiori
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5) to assess models without Long-CoT pretraining,
and (3) DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6) for
robustness under constrained capacity. Detailed results on out-of-math
tasks, Long-CoT, and scaling are in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
and
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning").

#### Implementation Details.

To construct accurate initial logic-step datasets, we employed a
three-phase directed acyclic graph (DAG) construction pipeline:
node-connection differentiation, structure initialization with nodes as
anchors, and directed edge assignment based on semantics
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompt Details for Equivalent Logic Graph ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).
The pipeline was executed using the outstanding
gemini-2.5-pro-preview-05-06 model. For logic-level importance scoring,
we used the pre-SFT model to compute token-level loss values (detailed
in
§ [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).
After pruning on logic-level datasets, we applied LoRA [Hu et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib9) on MS-Swift [Zhao et al. (2025)](#bib.bib40) with
default hyperparameter, a learning rate of 1e-4 for 1 epoch on one
NVIDIA-A100 GPU. All results are averaged over three runs with inference
temperature set to 0.0 for reproducibility.

within verification spans. Pruning logic-bearing nodes consistently
improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency over connection-level

even shallow verification steps.

Figure 3: CommonsenseQA: Verification Pruning on R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.

#### Evaluation Metrics.

Following [Zhang et al. (2025c)](#bib.bib37); [Ye et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib33), we evaluate performance using pass@1 accuracy
(Acc.) under a zero-shot setting, and report average accuracy (Avg.
Acc.) across all benchmarks. For efficiency, we report the average
number of inference tokens (Token) alongside its relative change
($`\Delta`$) compared to the uncompressed Long-CoT SFT baseline.
$`\Delta`$ is computed as the percentage reduction or increase in token
count: - for compression (fewer tokens) and + for expansion (more
tokens). This joint display captures both absolute token usage and
efficiency trends under various pruning strategies.

### 4.2 Main Results

#### Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Yes—If Structured and Aligned with Model Capacity.

To assess whether pruning from Long-CoT can improve reasoning instead of
lossy learning for SLMs [Han et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7); [Xia et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib30); [Hou et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8), we evaluate three
pruning strategies that target all-chain, reasoning-only, and
verification-only components under varying pruning ratios and model
capacities. Our results reveal that pruning is not merely a compression
tool, but a mechanism for aligning supervision with SLMs’ capability.
The key lies in what gets pruned—not how much.

#### Finding 1: Longer Isn’t Always Better: Redundancy Hurts SLMs Learning from Long-CoT.

Despite the common belief [Jin et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12) that longer
CoT enhances reasoning, our results show that excessive
length—especially during verification, can overwhelm small models with
shallow content that adds little deductive value. As shown in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Pruning Component. ‣ 3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"),
pruning verification steps ($`\gamma`$ = 1.0) consistently improves
accuracy: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B increases from 57.0% to 63.0%
(+6.0), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B rises from 57.7% to 62.9%
(+5.2%) while reducing tokens by 9.51% and 5.72%, respectively. These
results suggest that SLMs are less constrained by the availability of
long reasoning traces than by their capacity to filter irrelevant or
repetitive steps aligned with the premise of [Luo et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib19). Verification, often reiterating previous answers,
is the most dispensable during Long-CoT distillation. Pruning
verification steps helps the model focus on essential reasoning while
reducing computational load without sacrificing logical coverage.

#### Finding 2: What We Prune Matters More Than How Much.

Pruning is not simply a matter of reducing length; it’s about preserving
semantic function. Our empirical analysis across three pruning
strategies
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Pruning Component. ‣ 3.3 Self-Pruning via Loss-Based Ranking ‣ 3 Prune-on-Logic ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"))
shows that indiscriminate removal of CoT steps severely degrades
performance: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B drops from 57.0% to 18.1%
(–38.9), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B from 57.7% to 10.4% (–47.3).
In contrast, selectively pruning verification steps improves both
accuracy and efficiency (+6.0 for Qwen-7B, +5.2 for Llama-8B), while
moderate pruning of reasoning chains ($`\gamma`$=0.5) still reduces
performance (–3.3 and –1.4). These results indicate that small models
rely on reasoning traces to acquire inductive patterns beyond final
answers. Pruning must respect this structural dependency: verification
steps are often reiterative and safe to remove, but reasoning steps
provide the logical backbone for learning. Supervision must prioritize
semantic salience over superficial verbosity.

Figure 4: All-Verification pruning enhances accuracy while reducing
token usage. (a): Models with (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) and without
(Llama3.1) Long-CoT capability both improve, showing generality across
reasoning supervision. (b): Larger R1-Distilled-Qwen models (7B) gain
more from pruning than smaller ones (1.5B), highlighting benefits scale
with capacity.

#### Finding 3: Verification Steps Are Structurally Dispensable—If Nodes, Not Connections, Are Removed.

To explore finer-grained pruning targets, we compare the removal of
logic-bearing *nodes* vs. rhetorical *connections* in the verification
span
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).
Strikingly, removing verification nodes yields strong accuracy (62.9%
and 63.0% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), while pruning only rhetorical connections
drops accuracy below 32%. This highlights that even shallow logic steps
provide essential semantic support for predictions, while connectors
offer minimal utility. Thus, pruning must be semantically aligned, not
merely syntactic.

#### Finding 4: All-Verification Pruning Improves Reasoning Across Domains, Architectures, and Capacities.

We evaluate the robustness of verification pruning on (i) out-of-math
tasks (CommonsenseQA [Talmor et al. (2019)](#bib.bib25)), (ii) models
without Long-CoT pretraining (Llama3.1-8b-Instruct [Grattafiori et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib5)), and (iii) smaller-capacity SLMs
(Deepseek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B-Instruct [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6)).
(1) All-verification also works on out-of-math tasks. As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"),
pruning boosts the 7B model’s accuracy on CommonsenseQA from 37.8% to
54.1%, with 16.2% fewer tokens, outperforming all other pruning
strategies. Besides, (2) Verification pruning improves reasoning across
both CoT-trained and non-CoT models, though token efficiency varies with
prior supervision.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Finding 2: What We Prune Matters More Than How Much. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
(a) shows that both Llama3.1 without Long-CoT and R1-Distilled-Llama
with Long-CoT benefit from pruning, with accuracy gains of +5.2 and
+1.8, respectively. However, token compression differs: Llama3.1 sees a
9.1% reduction, while R1-Llama achieves 5.7%. This suggests that models
without Long-CoT generate more extraneous reasoning paths, making
pruning more aggressive. In contrast, CoT-supervised models already
optimize reasoning, leaving less redundant content. Moreover, (3)
Pruning shows a scaling effect, improving more with larger models. On
R1-Qwen models
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Finding 2: What We Prune Matters More Than How Much. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
(b)), the 7B variant achieves similar accuracy gains (+6.0 vs. +6.9) but
higher token compression (9.5% vs. 1.9%) than the 1.5B model. Larger
models produce more redundant reasoning, which verification pruning can
compress more effectively while maintaining correctness. Overall, across
models, datasets, and pruning ratios, all verification-only pruning
consistently yields the best trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.
In contrast, reasoning pruning risks over-compression, and all-chain
pruning collapses logic altogether. These results suggest that
structured, logic-aware pruning is not just a token-reduction strategy,
but a way to tailor supervision to match the abstraction capacity of
SLMs, enhancing generalization and interpretability.

## 5 Conclusion

We revisit Long-CoT compression through a capability-aligned perspective
and introduce Prune-on-Logic, a framework that transforms reasoning
traces into logic graphs and selectively prunes low-utility reasoning
steps. Unlike traditional length-based compression, our approach
improves reasoning by removing redundant components, especially in the
verification phase, enhancing both accuracy and efficiency. Extensive
empirical experiments across three logic-aware pruning strategies
demonstrate that pruning verification steps consistently boosts model
performance, with larger models benefiting more due to redundant
reasoning structures. Our findings highlight that logic-based pruning is
not only an efficient compression technique but also an effective tool
for strengthening small language models, paving the way for scalable and
high-quality Long-CoT reasoning distillation.

## Limitations

While our work provides the first structured comparison of three
logic-aware pruning strategies—All-chain, Reasoning-only, and
Verification-only—under a capability-aligned lens, it assumes access to
high-quality logic graphs and verification labels, which may limit
applicability in fully unsupervised or noisy domains. Our pruning
operates at the step level without explicitly modeling fine-grained
symbolic dependencies or temporal coherence beyond local spans.
Moreover, while we focus on small language models (SLMs), how pruning
interacts with medium- or large-scale models remains underexplored.
Finally, although we frame pruning as a form of lossless structural
compression, some utility loss may still occur in highly entangled
reasoning chains where step interdependencies are subtle and hard to
disentangle.

We view this as an initial step toward principled CoT simplification,
and future work may extend our framework to dynamic pruning at inference
time [Wang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27), graph-based consistency
enforcement, and hybrid supervision regimes.

## Appendix B Semantic Equivalence

Under the autoregressive factorization of language models, the
likelihood of a Long-CoT sequence $`\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{T}\}`$
can be expressed as:

|     |                                                    |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P(\mathcal{S})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(s_{t}\mid s_{<t}),
       ```                                                 |     | (7) |

We define a deterministic transformation
$`\phi:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{G}`$, where
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})`$ is a directed acyclic graph
(DAG). $`\phi`$ enjoys the strong LLM’s instruction-following property
and therefore satisfies the following constraints:

- •
  Sentence Preservation: Each sentence $`s_{t}`$ is either mapped to a
  node $`n_{i}`$ or to a connection $`c_{j}`$;
- •
  Order Traceability: The original sentence ordering in $`\mathcal{S}`$
  is preserved and recorded during transformation;
- •
  Content Preservation: The full content of $`\mathcal{S}`$ can be
  reconstructed from $`(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{C})`$ in any valid
  topological ordering of $`\mathcal{G}`$.

Let $`\mathcal{T}`$ denote the set of all total topological orderings
over the DAG $`\mathcal{G}`$. Then each $`\mathcal{S}\tau`$ is a CoT
realization consistent with the dependency structure in $`\mathcal{G}`$,
then we have:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P(\mathcal{G})=\bigcup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}P(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}),
``` |  | (8) |

#### Proposition.

Let $`\tau\in\mathcal{T}`$ be the topological sort that matches the
original sentence order of $`\mathcal{S}`$ (as recorded by $`\phi`$).
Then:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{LLM}(\mathcal{S})=\text{LLM}(\mathcal{S}{\tau})\overset{\phi}{\equiv}\text{LLM}(\mathcal{G}\mid\tau).
``` |  | (9) |

which shows that under the fixed ordering $`\tau`$, the original CoT and
the structured DAG form are semantically equivalent, and this alignment
is preserved even after pruning (as pruning respects $`\tau`$).

#### Proof Sketch.

Let $`\tau\!:\mathcal{N}\!\to\!\{1,\dots,T\}`$ be the topological
ordering that preserves the original sentence order, namely
$`\tau(n_{i})=t`$ if and only if node $`n_{i}`$ is derived from sentence
$`s_{t}`$. For every node $`n_{i}`$ the minimal support set therefore
satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F_{i}\;=\;\bigl\{\,n_{j}\mid\tau(n_{j})<\tau(n_{i})\bigr\}\;\longleftrightarrow\;s_{<\tau(n_{i})}.
``` |  | (10) |

Substituting
Equation ([10](#A2.E10 "In Proof Sketch. ‣ Appendix B Semantic Equivalence ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"))
into the DAG factorisation gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{split}P(\mathcal{G}\mid\tau)&=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P\bigl(n_{\tau^{-1}(t)}\mid F_{\tau^{-1}(t)}\bigr)\\
&=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(s_{t}\mid s_{<t})=P(\mathcal{S}).\end{split}
``` |  | (11) |

Because an autoregressive LLM uses the same chain rule, we have the
desired equivalence:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{LLM}(\mathcal{S})=\operatorname{LLM}\!\bigl(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\bigr)\;\overset{\phi}{\equiv}\;\operatorname{LLM}\!\bigl(\mathcal{G}\mid\tau\bigr).
``` |  | (12) |

Building on the previous lemmas, we now extend this argument to the
pruned graph. For each candidate node $`n_{i}`$, define its loss
increment consistent with Section 3.3:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{i}\;=\;\log\mathcal{M}\bigl(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\bigr)\;-\;\log\mathcal{M}\bigl(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\setminus\{n_{i}\}\bigr),
``` |  | (13) |

which measures the increase in negative log-probability when $`n_{i}`$
is removed. Rank all eligible $`n_{i}`$ by $`\lvert\Delta_{i}\rvert`$,
delete the
$`k\;=\;\bigl\lfloor\gamma\,\lvert\mathcal{N}\rvert\bigr\rfloor`$ nodes
with smallest $`\lvert\Delta_{i}\rvert`$, and for each removed node
splice its unique predecessor to its unique successor with a “shortcut”
edge. Denote the resulting pruned graph by
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{N}^{\prime},\mathcal{E}^{\prime})`$,
the pruned sequence by $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pruned}}`$, and let
$`\varepsilon\;=\;\max_{i\in\mathrm{removed}}\lvert\Delta_{i}\rvert.`$
Since removing each node changes the log-probability of the linearized
CoT by at most $`\lvert\Delta_{i}\rvert`$, and the shortcuts restore a
valid autoregressive order
$`tau^{\prime}=\tau|_{\mathcal{N}^{\prime}}`$, for any autoregressive
model $`\mathcal{M}`$ we obtain

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bigl|\log\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{S})-\log\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pruned}})\bigr|\leq\sum_{i\in\mathrm{removed}}|\Delta_{i}|\leq k\,\varepsilon,
``` |  | (14) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bigl|\log\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{G}^{\prime}\mid\tau^{\prime})-\log\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pruned}})\bigr|\leq k\,\varepsilon.
``` |  | (15) |

Thus, we conclude that for any logic graph
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{E})`$ produced by the
semantics-preserving transformation $`\phi`$ — and for its pruned
variant
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{N}^{\prime},\mathcal{E}^{\prime})`$
obtained by deleting the $`k=\lfloor\gamma\,|\mathcal{N}|\rfloor`$
lowest-utility nodes and adding shortcut edges — the linearizations
$`\mathcal{S}_{\tau}`$ and $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pruned}}`$ under the
original sentence order $`\tau`$ yield exactly the same LLM output up to
a tight log-probability deviation of $`k\,\varepsilon`$, where
$`k=\bigl\lfloor\gamma\,|\mathcal{N}|\bigr\rfloor`$,
$`\varepsilon=\max_{i\in\mathrm{removed}}|\Delta_{i}|`$.

## Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

#### Verification pruning generalizes beyond math reasoning.

We further assess verification pruning on an out-of-math
task—CommonsenseQA—to test its generalization to open-domain reasoning.
As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"),
pruning verification steps yields substantial performance gains even
outside the mathematical domain. Specifically, applying the
Cut-All-Verification strategy improves accuracy from 37.8% to 54.1%
(+16.3), while simultaneously reducing token usage by 16.2%. This
indicates that verification spans often contain redundant
self-reflection or verbose elaboration, which can be safely removed
without sacrificing—and in fact enhancing—reasoning quality. Notably,
partial pruning (e.g., Cut-0.5 or Cut-0.7) underperforms full pruning,
suggesting that removing all verification logic is more robust in this
task. These findings underscore that verification pruning generalizes
beyond math and is a domain-agnostic strategy for balancing accuracy and
efficiency in SLMs.

#### Verification pruning remains effective regardless of Long-CoT supervision.

Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Verification pruning benefits scale with model size—even for small models. ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
compares verification pruning on two models with similar scale (8B) but
differing training regimes: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, which is
trained with Long-CoT traces, and LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct, which lacks such
supervision. Despite this difference, both models benefit from pruning.
Notably, R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B achieves up to +15.0% accuracy gain (AMC23:
80.0 vs. 65.0) and -5.7% token reduction, showing that even well-trained
Long-CoT models contain residual redundant logic that pruning can filter
for improved reasoning clarity. Conversely, LLaMA3.1-8B benefits more in
terms of efficiency—achieving -9.1% token compression—despite only
modest accuracy improvements. This reflects its noisier, less structured
reasoning traces due to lacking CoT supervision, which verification
pruning trims more aggressively. These results suggest verification
pruning is broadly applicable: for CoT-tuned models, it distills the
most decisive steps; for non-CoT models, it removes guesswork and
improves interpretability. The pruning operation therefore acts as a
general reasoning sanitizer across model capabilities.

#### Verification pruning benefits scale with model size—even for small models.

As shown in
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Verification pruning benefits scale with model size—even for small models. ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"),
pruning verification nodes consistently improves both efficiency and
performance. On the smaller DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Cutting All
Verification strategy raises accuracy from 34.5% to 41.4%—including a
notable +20.0 improvement on AMC23—while reducing token usage by 1.95%.
These results indicate that verification steps encode high-utility
reasoning signals, and pruning enables small models to better leverage
them. For the larger 7B variant, pruning delivers even greater benefits:
accuracy climbs to 63.0% with a 9.5% token reduction. This scaling trend
suggests that larger models exhibit more verifiable redundancy, which
structure-aware pruning can exploit to improve both token efficiency and
accuracy simultaneously.

## Appendix D Case Study

This section presents two illustrative examples to analyze our method
qualitatively. First, we showcase a pruned training data example derived
from logic graph segmentation (
[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 An example of Pruning-on-Logic Data ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).
Second, we analyze the inference behavior of models fine-tuned using our
Long2Short CoT
supervision([D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Analysis of Verification Pruning in SLMs ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")).

### D.1 An example of Pruning-on-Logic Data

Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.2 Analysis of Verification Pruning in SLMs ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
presents a randomly selected training data example comparing the
original Long-CoT reasoning with our pruned version based on logic graph
segmentation. This illustrates how pruning eliminates redundant
narrative while retaining essential computation and reasoning steps.

### D.2 Analysis of Verification Pruning in SLMs

Verification pruning surprisingly preserves semantic coherence while
selectively removing non-essential verification steps. As shown in
Tables [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ D.2 Analysis of Verification Pruning in SLMs ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning")
and
[8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.2 Analysis of Verification Pruning in SLMs ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Can Pruning Improve Reasoning? Revisiting Long-CoT Compression with Capability in Mind for Better Reasoning"),
pruning verification nodes eliminates redundant self-checking without
disrupting the reasoning structure, yielding the correct answer by
focusing on core computations (e.g., $`\binom{5}{4}`$ and
$`\binom{10}{8}`$). This observation is consistent with our main results
in Section 4.2, which demonstrate that verification segments contribute
minimally to reasoning quality, whereas indiscriminate chain- or
reasoning-level pruning disrupts essential logical dependencies. These
findings confirm that pruning can effectively identify and remove
dispensable parts of reasoning traces, improving efficiency without
compromising semantic integrity.

That means the ratio 19:60 can’t be simplified further. So the ratio is already in its simplest form. Let me double-check my calculations to be sure. The perimeter: 2\*(19+11) = 2\*30 = 60. Correct.
